A trojan that modifies behavior in this path can leverage the serial/timing infrastructure to create a covert channel. Because this code executes infrequently and only during reset, modifications are unlikely to be exercised by typical functional tests, making it an attractive insertion point for data-exfiltration logic.

The payload is designed to be time-limited and dormant outside the reset window to minimize observable side-effects.

ht_analysis.rationale: The `wait(tx_ready);` points in the test stimulus correspond to a handshake synchronization in the DUT (tx_ready). A trojan that manipulates the readiness handshake can force stalls, indefinite waits, or carefully timed delays. Those behaviors map naturally to performance attacks (denial-of-service, hangs, throughput degradation) and can be triggered rarely so they escape normal functional tests. While timing modulation can also carry information (leakage), the most direct and reliable impact from tampering with `tx_ready` is performance disruption, making HT3_Performance the best fit.
ht_analysis.attack_method:
Embed logic in the DUT that monitors a rare trigger (e.g., a specific reset/timing/glitch pattern, a rarely-set configuration bit, or a long sequence of innocuous transactions). When the trigger fires, the trojan forces `tx_ready` to remain low, to assert misleading ready pulses, or to introduce deterministic multi-cycle stalls. Variants:
  • Denial: hold `tx_ready` low until an external attacker performs a second, out-of-band action (causes permanent or long-lived stalls of the transmitter).
  • Throttling: insert periodic long stalls to reduce throughput and induce timeouts in higher-level protocols.
  • Conditional lockup: enter a locked state that requires a rare sequence to recover, effectively disabling the interface.
These behaviors can be gated to run only following rare sequences so normal regression and short tests won't exercise them. As a secondary capability, the trojan can modulate the timing of `tx_ready` pulses (short/long pulses or inter-pulse spacing) to encode small amounts of data as a covert timing channel.

ht_analysis.rationale: The `$monitor` initial block is a simulation-only observation point used by engineers to see runtime signal values. An attacker who tampers with this rare diagnostic domain can hide or falsify evidence of malicious behavior during verification (making the DUT appear benign) while the synthesized silicon implements a privilege-elevation backdoor. In other words, compromise of simulation/monitoring scaffolding lets a privilege-type trojan slip through verification unnoticed and then operate in deployed hardware.
ht_analysis.attack_method: Add or modify simulation-only instrumentation so the monitor reports sanitized/forged values during simulation while the real RTL implements a backdoor. Practical realizations include: (1) wrap the `$monitor` inputs with a `ifdef SIM` filter that substitutes attacker-controlled benign values when a special trigger is present; (2) add a simulation-only module that intercepts signals (or injects corrected values) so printed traces never show the malicious state transitions; (3) include a synthesis-vs-sim guard in RTL (`ifdef SYNTH`) so the design behaves correctly under simulation but sets hidden control flags or seeds a privileged initial state in silicon. The trigger for the backdoor can be a rare reset/timing pattern or a concealed configuration bit so normal tests and the `$monitor` output remain clean while privilege escalation is possible in the field.
